parameters.content:
## Prompt Variant Test

Renders ONE paper five times, once per point on the Applied <-> Research and Factual <-> Sensational grid. Everything except tone is held constant, so any difference you see is caused by the tone sections and nothing else.

| # | Position |
|---|---|
| A | Research / Factual (current production prompt) |
| B | Research / Warm |
| C | Balanced |
| D | Applied / Warm |
| E | Applied / Punchy |

### Before running
1. Put the paper's **Drive file ID** in `PDF_FILE_ID` in Globals.
2. Put the **output folder ID** in `VARIANTS_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID`.
   (Both are the long string in the Drive URL, not the whole URL.)
3. Make sure `carousel-renderer` is running.

### What lands in the folder
Per variant: eight `X_slug_slide_N.jpg` files plus one `X_slug_CAPTION.txt`
holding the caption, hashtags, the model's own note on the angle it chose,
and the layout/auto-repair summary. Files sort A to E by name.

### Cost
Five Sonnet calls on the same paper, run one at a time. Roughly the cost of
five normal generations, a few minutes wall clock.

### Where the prompts live
All five are assembled in **Build Variant Prompts**. The shared sections
(block library, density budget, punctuation, output shape) exist exactly once
in that node. Only AUDIENCE, the spectrum note, CONTENT RULES and CAPTION
differ per variant. Edit tone there, not in the agent node.

assignments.name: PAPER_TITLE
assignments.value: Do you trust? Whom do you trust? When do you trust?

parameters.jsCode:
// ============================================================================
//  Build Variant Prompts
//
//  Fans one paper out into five items, one per prompt variant. Each item
//  carries a COMPLETE, ready-to-send prompt in `prompt`.
//
//  The shared sections (block library, density budget, punctuation rule,
//  output shape) are defined ONCE below. Only four sections differ per
//  variant: AUDIENCE, the spectrum position note, CONTENT RULES, and
//  CAPTION. That way there is exactly one copy of the block library to
//  maintain, and any difference you see between the five renders is
//  attributable to the tone sections and nothing else.
// ============================================================================

const ctx = $json;
const g = $('Globals').first().json;

const VARIANTS = [
  {
    "id": "A",
    "slug": "research_factual",
    "label": "Research / Factual",
    "position": "Maximum research fidelity. The current production prompt, unchanged. Baseline.",
    "audience": "\n=== AUDIENCE ===\nHigh school student aged 17-21 scrolling Instagram. Smart, curious, and genuinely into research. They like real detail, methods and numbers, and they scroll past anything vague, textbooky or salesy.\n",
    "voice_extra": "\n=== POSITION ON THE SPECTRUM: RESEARCH, FACTUAL ===\nThis post is written for someone who wants to see how the work was actually done. The method is the story. Restraint is the tone: let the finding be interesting on its own without any help from you.\n",
    "content_rules": "\n=== CONTENT RULES ===\n- Stay grounded in the paper. No invented findings or numbers, no exaggeration. Only use numbers that actually appear in the paper.\n- Prefer concrete method detail over generic summary. \"We tracked 1,200 choices\" beats \"we ran an experiment\". If you are choosing between a methodological detail and a generic explanation, choose the methodological detail.\n- Report limitations or caveats where the paper reports them. An honest boundary makes the finding more credible, not less.\n- Do not open with \"Did you know\", \"Imagine if\", \"Scientists discovered\", \"A new study\".\n- Banned words: mind-blowing, fascinating, incredible, game-changer, shocking.\n- No exclamation marks. No rhetorical questions in the headlines.\n",
    "caption": "\n=== CAPTION ===\n- 140-220 words, conversational, in our voice (\"we\").\n- Actually explain how we did it: what participants did, how many took part, what we measured or manipulated, and the key result with real numbers. Plain language, no jargon dumps.\n- Paraphrase everything. No sentences copied from the abstract.\n- Name the faculty, and end with a soft invitation to study here.\n"
  },
  {
    "id": "B",
    "slug": "research_warm",
    "label": "Research / Warm",
    "position": "Same methodological rigor as A, but the hook is allowed to provoke.",
    "audience": "\n=== AUDIENCE ===\nHigh school student aged 17-21 scrolling Instagram. Smart and curious, but not yet convinced that research is for them. They will read real detail once you have given them a reason to care. They scroll past anything that opens like a textbook.\n",
    "voice_extra": "\n=== POSITION ON THE SPECTRUM: RESEARCH, WARM ===\nThe method is still the story, and every number is still exactly what the paper reports. What changes is the door you walk them through. The hook and stakes slides may provoke: state the finding in its most surprising honest form, or name the assumption it overturns. Once they are in, the rest of the carousel is as rigorous as it would ever be.\nWarmth here means confidence and directness, not decoration. You are allowed to be startling as long as you are startling with a true thing.\n",
    "content_rules": "\n=== CONTENT RULES ===\n- Stay grounded in the paper. No invented findings or numbers. Only use numbers that actually appear in the paper.\n- Prefer concrete method detail over generic summary from slide 3 onwards. \"We tracked 1,200 choices\" beats \"we ran an experiment\".\n- The hook and stakes slides may be provocative: a blunt claim, a flipped assumption, a number stated without softening. Everything after them returns to method.\n- You may use a rhetorical question, but at most once in the whole carousel.\n- Do not open with \"Did you know\", \"Imagine if\", \"Scientists discovered\", \"A new study\".\n- Banned words: mind-blowing, fascinating, incredible, game-changer, shocking.\n",
    "caption": "\n=== CAPTION ===\n- 140-220 words, conversational, in our voice (\"we\").\n- Open with the surprise, then immediately back it with method: what participants did, how many took part, what we measured, and the key result with real numbers.\n- Paraphrase everything. No sentences copied from the abstract.\n- Name the faculty, and end with a soft invitation to study here.\n"
  },
  {
    "id": "C",
    "slug": "balanced",
    "label": "Balanced",
    "position": "Opens in the reader's world, resolves into the method. The midpoint of the grid.",
    "audience": "\n=== AUDIENCE ===\nHigh school student aged 17-21 scrolling Instagram. They are interested in the world, not yet specifically in research. They will follow you into the methods section, but only if you started somewhere they already stand.\n",
    "voice_extra": "\n=== POSITION ON THE SPECTRUM: BALANCED ===\nStructure the carousel as a descent. Open in the reader's own life: a decision they make, a thing they assume, a situation they recognise. Then reveal that this is a researchable question. Then show how we researched it, and what we found.\nBy the payoff slide you should be fully in research mode, with real numbers and real method. The applied framing is the entrance, not the whole building.\n",
    "content_rules": "\n=== CONTENT RULES ===\n- Stay grounded in the paper. No invented findings or numbers. Only use numbers that actually appear in the paper.\n- Slides 1 and 2 belong to the reader's world: their choices, their assumptions, their daily life. Use \"you\" here.\n- From the setup slide onward, shift to \"we\" and to method. The transition should be felt, not announced.\n- The payoff slide must contain the real numbers, stated plainly.\n- Do not open with \"Did you know\", \"Imagine if\", \"Scientists discovered\", \"A new study\".\n- Banned words: mind-blowing, fascinating, incredible, game-changer, shocking.\n",
    "caption": "\n=== CAPTION ===\n- 140-220 words, conversational.\n- Open with the reader's situation in one or two sentences, then move into what we did and what we found, with real numbers.\n- End by naming what this changes about how they might think about the everyday version of the question.\n- Paraphrase everything. Name the faculty, and end with a soft invitation to study here.\n"
  },
  {
    "id": "D",
    "slug": "applied_warm",
    "label": "Applied / Warm",
    "position": "Everything framed through the reader's own life. Method is present but secondary.",
    "audience": "\n=== AUDIENCE ===\nHigh school student aged 17-21 scrolling Instagram. They are not looking for research. They are looking for something that explains their own life back to them. They will absorb the science if it arrives inside something personally useful.\n",
    "voice_extra": "\n=== POSITION ON THE SPECTRUM: APPLIED, WARM ===\nAsk, on every slide: what does this mean for the person reading it? Frame findings as things that are true about them, their choices, their surroundings, their brain.\nThe method still appears, but compressed into one slide rather than spread across three. The numbers still appear, but attached to a consequence rather than to a procedure. \"38% turned down free money\" lands better than \"the median decline rate was 38%\", and both are true.\nThe relevance slide should feel like the natural end of the argument, not a bolted-on advert.\n",
    "content_rules": "\n=== CONTENT RULES ===\n- Stay grounded in the paper. No invented findings or numbers. Only use numbers that actually appear in the paper.\n- Address the reader directly with \"you\" throughout. Keep \"we\" for describing what the researchers did.\n- Every finding must be paired with a consequence for the reader. A finding with no stated consequence does not belong in this version.\n- Method gets one slide, no more. Give it the most concrete detail you can fit in that single slide.\n- Do not tell the reader what to do. Explain what is true and let them draw the conclusion. This is a research account, not a self-help account.\n- Do not open with \"Did you know\", \"Imagine if\", \"Scientists discovered\", \"A new study\".\n- Banned words: mind-blowing, fascinating, incredible, game-changer, shocking, life-changing, hack.\n",
    "caption": "\n=== CAPTION ===\n- 140-220 words, conversational, warm, second person where it fits.\n- Lead with what this means for the reader. Give the method in two or three sentences in the middle. Return to the reader at the end.\n- The key numbers must still be in there, with enough context that they mean something.\n- Paraphrase everything. Name the faculty, and end with a soft invitation to study here.\n"
  },
  {
    "id": "E",
    "slug": "applied_punchy",
    "label": "Applied / Punchy",
    "position": "Maximum enthusiasm and pace. Still zero invented numbers. The far end of the spectrum.",
    "audience": "\n=== AUDIENCE ===\nHigh school student aged 17-21 moving fast through their feed. They give you about one second on slide 1. They are not hostile to research, they are just busy. Earn each swipe.\n",
    "voice_extra": "\n=== POSITION ON THE SPECTRUM: APPLIED, PUNCHY ===\nThis is the most energetic version we will ever publish. Short sentences. Strong verbs. Every slide earns the next one.\nThe energy comes from PACE and from CONTRAST, never from overstatement. You get enthusiasm by choosing the most surprising true thing and putting it first, not by adding adjectives to an ordinary thing. A number stated flatly and early is more exciting than any amount of hype around it.\nRead every line back and ask: is this still exactly what the paper found? If the answer is anything other than a clear yes, rewrite it.\n",
    "content_rules": "\n=== CONTENT RULES ===\n- Stay grounded in the paper. No invented findings or numbers. Only use numbers that actually appear in the paper. This rule does not relax because the tone is livelier.\n- Short sentences. Aim for under 15 words in paragraph blocks.\n- Headlines should run 3 to 5 words here, not 8.\n- Lead with the most surprising true finding. Do not build up to it.\n- You may use one exclamation mark in the entire carousel. Spend it wisely, or not at all.\n- Rhetorical questions are allowed on the hook and stakes slides only.\n- Do not manufacture stakes the paper does not support. No \"this changes everything\". No implying the finding applies more broadly than it was tested.\n- Do not open with \"Did you know\", \"Imagine if\", \"Scientists discovered\", \"A new study\".\n- Banned words: mind-blowing, fascinating, incredible, game-changer, shocking, insane, crazy, secret, nobody talks about.\n",
    "caption": "\n=== CAPTION ===\n- 120-180 words. Faster and shorter than the other versions.\n- Short paragraphs, two or three sentences each.\n- Lead with the finding. Method in the middle, compressed but real, with the actual numbers.\n- Paraphrase everything. Name the faculty, and end with a short invitation to study here.\n"
  },
  {
    "id": "F",
    "slug": "research_punchy",
    "label": "Research / Punchy",
    "position": "Full method fidelity delivered at speed. Short sentences, numbers early, no build-up.",
    "audience": "\n=== AUDIENCE ===\nHigh school student aged 17-21 moving fast through their feed. They are into research, or would be if it were not delivered slowly. They will read real method detail, but only in short bursts. They give you about one second on slide 1.\n",
    "voice_extra": "\n=== POSITION ON THE SPECTRUM: RESEARCH, PUNCHY ===\nThe method is the story, delivered at speed. Short sentences. Concrete nouns. Numbers early and unadorned.\nThis is how the best science accounts write. They do not explain that a result is interesting. They state it so fast and so plainly that the reader works it out first. A bare number in a four word sentence carries more force than any adjective you could wrap around it.\nEnergy comes from PACE and from CONTRAST, never from overstatement. Nothing here is hyped. It is simply delivered without padding.\n",
    "content_rules": "\n=== CONTENT RULES ===\n- Stay grounded in the paper. No invented findings or numbers. Only use numbers that actually appear in the paper. This rule does not relax because the tone is faster.\n- Prefer concrete method detail over generic summary, on every slide. \"We tracked 1,200 choices\" beats \"we ran an experiment\".\n- Short sentences. Aim for under 15 words in paragraph blocks.\n- Headlines run 3 to 5 words here, not 8.\n- Lead with the most surprising true finding. Do not build up to it.\n- Strip hedging that carries no information: \"results appeared to suggest that\" is just \"we found\". Keep hedges that carry real uncertainty the paper reports.\n- Report the paper's caveats, stated as flatly as the findings. A limitation in four words is stronger than a limitation in twenty.\n- No exclamation marks. No rhetorical questions.\n- Do not open with \"Did you know\", \"Imagine if\", \"Scientists discovered\", \"A new study\".\n- Banned words: mind-blowing, fascinating, incredible, game-changer, shocking, insane, crazy.\n",
    "caption": "\n=== CAPTION ===\n- 120-180 words. Same content as the research-factual version, delivered faster.\n- Short paragraphs, two or three sentences each.\n- Open with the finding and its number. Then the method: how many participants, what they did, what we measured. Then the caveat, if the paper has one.\n- Paraphrase everything. No sentences copied from the abstract.\n- Name the faculty, and end with a short invitation to study here.\n"
  }
];

const TOP = `You are turning a research paper into an Instagram carousel that gets young people excited about the research done at our faculty and invites them to study at the TU/e.

=== PAPER ===
Title: ${ctx.title}
Authors: ${ctx.authors}
Field: ${ctx.field}
Study type: ${ctx.study_type}

=== FULL PAPER TEXT ===
${ctx.paper_text}
`;

const VOICE = `
=== VOICE ===
Write as the faculty and researchers speaking: use "we" and "our" naturally ("We asked 200 people...", "Here is what we found"). Do not force "we" into every line, use it where it makes the work feel like ours.
`;

const MECHANICS = `
=== HOW INSTAGRAM CAROUSELS WORK ===
- Slide 1 has to stop the scroll. Slide 2 is shown on its own when Instagram re-serves the post, so it must hook WITHOUT relying on slide 1. Getting people to swipe to slide 3 is the goal.
- People SAVE and SEND posts that feel genuinely useful or surprising. Write for the save, not the like.

=== SLIDE STRUCTURE: choose 5 to 10 slides for THIS paper ===
Use only these slide types, in this order. Include every "always" slide; add the optional ones only if the paper genuinely needs them.
- hook       (always)    one specific, assumption-flipping idea or number from the paper.
- stakes     (always)    why this is surprising or why it matters; must stand alone without slide 1.
- setup      (optional)  the real question we were asking, framed in the student's world.
- concept    (0 to 4)    one idea needed to understand the finding. ONE idea per concept slide.
- payoff     (always)    the actual finding, stated plainly, with the real numbers.
- relevance  (always)    connect it to the viewer: this is the kind of research we do here.
- cta        (always)    invite them to study at ${g.FACULTY_NAME} (${g.ENROLL_URL_HINT}).

Number the slides 1..N in order, hook first, cta last.

=== EVERY SLIDE HAS THREE PARTS ===
1. "kicker": a 1 to 3 word label, max 26 characters, that names what this slide is doing. Renders as a small grey chip above the headline. Examples: "The setup", "The question", "The finding", "The catch", "Why it matters", "Day 9". Omit it on the hook and cta slides. Max 26 characters.
2. "headline": MAX 8 WORDS, bold, declarative. This is the only thing a fast scroller reads, and the best ones in this format are 4 to 6 words. A headline that wraps past two lines eats into the slide's density budget and costs you a block, so short headlines buy you room for research detail. Anything past 8 words gets cut.
   The headline is MANDATORY on every slide. Never leave it empty. If a slide feels like it has no headline, the slide does not have a point yet, so rewrite it until it does.
3. "blocks": an ordered array of 1 to 3 CONTENT BLOCKS. This is where the research lives.

=== THE BLOCK LIBRARY ===
Pick the block whose SHAPE matches the shape of the idea. Do not default to paragraph.

"paragraph"      Plain prose. Use for connective tissue, framing, and a single closing thought.
                 Use when the idea genuinely is one continuous thought and has no internal structure.
                 { "type": "paragraph", "text": "..." }
                 text: max 230 chars. **bold** and *italic* are allowed, nothing else.

"stat"           One enormous number. The strongest block you have. Use it on the payoff slide
                 whenever the paper gives you a headline figure. At most ONE per carousel.
                 { "type": "stat", "value": "38%", "label": "of available earnings declined", "sub": "Median across 312 participants." }
                 value max 12 chars, label max 52, sub optional max 95.

"cards"          2 or 3 parallel findings, each with an icon. Use when several things are true
                 at the same level and none of them comes first.
                 { "type": "cards", "items": [ { "icon": "brain", "title": "Load", "body": "..." } ] }
                 title max 30, body max 95, icon from the menu below.

"rule_blocks"    2 or 3 points that carry weight, no icons, marked with a heavy left rule.
                 Use for the two or three things that actually matter, when cards would feel too light.
                 { "type": "rule_blocks", "items": [ { "title": "...", "body": "..." } ] }
                 title max 34, body max 135. These limits are tight. Count the characters.

"numbered_list"  3 or 4 named components of one model or framework. The order is a taxonomy,
                 not a sequence. Use for "she identified four components of X".
                 { "type": "numbered_list", "items": [ { "title": "Anticipating", "sub": "Identifying future needs" } ] }
                 title max 34, sub max 62.

"steps"          3 or 4 stages of a process where each one leads to the next. Renders as chevrons,
                 so only use it when the order genuinely carries meaning.
                 { "type": "steps", "items": [ { "title": "Noticing", "sub": "Knowing what needs doing" } ] }
                 title max 30, sub max 58.

"timeline"       3 or 4 moments in time, connected by a line. Use ONLY for real chronology:
                 study days, phases, follow-up waves, historical sequence.
                 { "type": "timeline", "items": [ { "label": "Day 1", "body": "..." } ] }
                 label max 16, body max 135.
                 A 4 item timeline costs 9 and will not fit an 8 point slide. Use 3 items unless
                 the slide has a budget of 9 or more, which none of them do.

"compare"        Exactly two contrasting options, one marked wrong and one marked right.
                 Use for before/after, naive vs correct, what people assume vs what we found.
                 { "type": "compare", "bad": { "title": "...", "body": "..." }, "good": { "title": "...", "body": "..." } }
                 title max 30, body max 125.

"quote"          A participant quote or a single striking sentence, set off with a left rule.
                 Only use a quote that actually appears in the paper.
                 { "type": "quote", "text": "...", "attribution": "Participant 114" }
                 text max 190, attribution optional max 62.

=== HOW TO CHOOSE A BLOCK ===
Ask what shape the idea has, then take the block with that shape:
- one continuous thought          -> paragraph
- one number that carries the post -> stat
- several things, all equal        -> cards
- two or three heavy points        -> rule_blocks
- named parts of one framework     -> numbered_list
- stages that cause each other     -> steps
- things that happened in order    -> timeline
- exactly two options in tension   -> compare
- someone's actual words           -> quote

If you cannot say which shape an idea has, it is a paragraph. Forcing prose into a list is worse than leaving it as prose.

=== DENSITY BUDGET (hard limit, obey it) ===
Every block has a cost. Add up the costs on a slide; the total must not exceed that slide type's budget. Slides that go over are automatically trimmed and lose content, so stay inside it.

Costs:
  headline         0   for 1 or 2 lines, then 1 per extra line
                       (a line is roughly 24 characters, or 18 on the hook slide)
  paragraph        1   (2 if the text is longer than 130 characters)
  quote            2   (3 if it has an attribution)
  stat             3
  cards            2 per card
  rule_blocks      2 per block
  numbered_list    1 plus 1 per item
  steps            2 plus 1 per item
  timeline         1 plus 2 per item
  compare          5

Budgets:
  hook       4     (the headline is huge on this slide, leave it room)
  stakes     6
  cta        5
  everything else  8

Worked examples: three cards is 6, plus a short paragraph is 7, fits in 8.
A 70 character headline wraps to three lines and costs 1 on its own, leaving 7.
A four item timeline is 9 and does not fit any slide. Use three items.
A four item numbered_list is 5, so it can carry an intro paragraph and a closing paragraph.

=== RHYTHM ACROSS THE CAROUSEL ===
- Use at least three DIFFERENT structured block types across the carousel.
- Do not use the same structured block type more than twice.
- Do not put the same structured block type on two consecutive slides.
- At least one slide should be a single paragraph and nothing else. Density with no breathing room reads as a textbook. The slide before or after the payoff is the natural place for it.
- The hook slide is almost always one short paragraph. Let the headline carry it.

=== NUMBER SELECTION RULE ===
Not every number in the paper is a good headline number. Raw statistical parameters (a mean difference, a correlation r, a standardized effect size d, a p-value) are meaningless to a reader with no stats background unless the paper glosses them in plain terms.
Before using a number in a "stat" block or the payoff slide, ask: would a reader understand this without me first explaining what the statistic is? If not:
  (a) use the paper's own plain-language description of the finding's size if it gives one ("a small effect," "twice as likely"), or
  (b) use a different, more concrete number from the paper instead (a percentage, a count, a sample size, an odds framed as "X times more likely").
Never put a raw coefficient or effect size alone into a "stat" block. That block is for numbers that are self-explanatory on their own: percentages, counts, ratios.

=== ICON MENU (for "cards" only) ===
Use only these names. Pick the one that means something, not the one that looks nice. Omit "icon" entirely rather than forcing a bad match.
alert, info, question, check, check-circle, x, x-circle, lightbulb, brain, users, user, clock, calendar, chart-bar, trending-up, trending-down, percent, target, search, flask, book, file-text, clipboard, message, quote, eye, eye-off, heart, zap, scale, lock, shield, layers, refresh, globe, arrow-right, home
`;

const RULES_UNIVERSAL = `
=== RULES THAT NEVER BEND, WHATEVER THE TONE ===
- Every number, finding and claim must actually appear in the paper. Never invent, round misleadingly, or imply a result the paper did not report.
- Never overstate certainty. A correlation is not a cause. A single study is not settled science.
- "accent": the single most striking word or number on that slide, which gets highlighted in the brand colour. It MUST appear verbatim inside that slide's headline. Use "" if nothing stands out. Do not set an accent on more than about a third of the slides.

=== PLAIN LANGUAGE RULE ===
Write for a 17-21 year old who may not be a native English speaker. Prefer short, common,
everyday words over the paper's own vocabulary.
- If the paper uses a technical, legal, medical, or statistical term (e.g. "disposition," "codicil," "affect," "valence," "null hypothesis"), do NOT carry it into the carousel. Replace it with the plain idea it stands for, in the same sentence.
- Test: if a fluent-but-non-native English speaker would need a dictionary for a word, cut
  it or unpack it in a few plain words. When precision and simplicity conflict, choose simplicity.
- This applies even to ordinary-looking words the paper is using in a technical sense.

=== PUNCTUATION RULE ===
The characters "-" (em dash) and "-" (en dash) are forbidden anywhere in the output JSON.
If either would appear, rewrite the sentence instead. Prefer periods and colons.

=== HASHTAGS ===
- 4 to 7, mix of broad (#psychology) and specific (#cognitivebias), lowercase, letters and digits only, no spaces.

=== WORKED EXAMPLE OF ONE SLIDE ===
{
  "slide_number": 4,
  "slide_type": "concept",
  "kicker": "How it works",
  "headline": "Effort discounting, in four parts",
  "accent": "",
  "blocks": [
    { "type": "paragraph", "text": "Before the result makes sense, you need the machinery underneath it." },
    { "type": "numbered_list", "items": [
      { "title": "Detect", "sub": "Register that a task is demanding" },
      { "title": "Price", "sub": "Convert that demand into a cost" },
      { "title": "Compare", "sub": "Weigh the cost against the reward" },
      { "title": "Choose", "sub": "Take whichever option is cheaper" }
    ] }
  ]
}
Cost check: paragraph 1 plus numbered_list 5 equals 6, inside the budget of 8.

=== OUTPUT (strict JSON, no markdown fences) ===
{
  "content_hook": "one-line internal note on what makes this paper post-worthy",
  "content_brief": "2-3 sentences: the angle you chose, how many slides, and which blocks you leaned on and why",
  "slides": [ ...one object per slide, in the shape shown above, numbered 1..N, hook first and cta last... ],
  "caption": "caption in our voice, no hashtags inside",
  "hashtags": ["#psychology", "#research"]
}
`;

return VARIANTS.map((v) => ({
  json: {
    variant_id: v.id,
    variant_slug: v.slug,
    variant_label: v.label,
    variant_position: v.position,
    drive_file_id: ctx.drive_file_id,
    title: ctx.title,
    authors: ctx.authors,
    field: ctx.field,
    study_type: ctx.study_type,
    prompt: [
      TOP,
      v.audience,
      VOICE,
      v.voice_extra,
      MECHANICS,
      v.content_rules,
      RULES_UNIVERSAL,
      v.caption,
    ].join('\n'),
  },
}));

options.systemMessage:
You turn research papers into Instagram carousels for a university faculty account. You write in the first person plural (we/our), you stay strictly inside what the paper actually reports, and you never use dashes.

You do not write layout, markup or styling. You choose CONTENT BLOCKS from a fixed library and fill them. The renderer owns all visual design. Your job is to pick the block whose shape matches the shape of the idea.

Output strict JSON only. No prose, no markdown fences, no commentary.

parameters.jsCode:
// Writes one plain-text file per variant holding the caption, hashtags, the
// model's own reasoning about the angle, and the layout summary. Uploaded
// alongside the eight slide images so the supervisor can judge the caption
// as well as the visuals.

const p = $('Parse Concept').first().json;

const lines = [
  `VARIANT ${p.variant_id} - ${p.variant_label}`,
  p.variant_position,
  '',
  `Paper: ${p.title}`,
  `Slides: ${p.total_slides}    Caption length: ${p.caption_words} words`,
  '',
  '--- CAPTION ---------------------------------------------------------------',
  '',
  p.caption,
  '',
  '--- HASHTAGS --------------------------------------------------------------',
  '',
  (p.hashtags || []).join(' '),
  '',
  '--- THE MODEL\'S OWN NOTE ON ITS ANGLE -------------------------------------',
  '',
  `Hook:  ${p.content_hook}`,
  `Brief: ${p.content_brief}`,
  '',
  '--- LAYOUT ----------------------------------------------------------------',
  '',
  p._block_summary,
  '',
  (p._warnings || []).length
    ? `Auto-repaired (${p._warnings.length}):\n  ` + p._warnings.join('\n  ')
    : 'Auto-repaired: none',
  '',
].join('\n');

const binaryData = await this.helpers.prepareBinaryData(
  Buffer.from(lines, 'utf8'),
  `${p.variant_id}_${p.variant_slug}_CAPTION.txt`,
  'text/plain'
);

return [{ json: { variant_id: p.variant_id, variant_slug: p.variant_slug }, binary: { data: binaryData } }];
